---
title: "Read your data"
description: "Turn a tracking export into an anipoint with aniread, and tell it about your recording."
order: 2
---



[aniread](https://animovement.dev/aniread) reads movement data from a wide range
of sources: pose estimation from video, centroid trackers, motion capture, even
trackball hardware. Whichever tool wrote the file, you get back the same
structure, so after this first step it stops mattering.

## What it can read {#sec-sources}

These are the sources aniread supports, with the reader for each and the file
types it accepts:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_supported_sources() |>
  print(n = Inf)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # A tibble: 18 x 3
#>    source           reader             suffix   
#>    <chr>            <chr>              <list>   
#>  1 aniframe         read_aniframe      <chr [1]>
#>  2 animalta         read_animalta      <chr [1]>
#>  3 anipose          read_anipose       <chr [1]>
#>  4 bonsai           read_bonsai        <chr [1]>
#>  5 boris            read_boris         <chr [2]>
#>  6 c3d              read_c3d           <chr [1]>
#>  7 deeplabcut       read_deeplabcut    <chr [2]>
#>  8 fasttrack        read_fasttrack     <chr [1]>
#>  9 fictrac          read_fictrac       <chr [1]>
#> 10 freemocap        read_freemocap     <chr [1]>
#> 11 idtrackerai      read_idtracker     <chr [2]>
#> 12 lightningpose    read_lightningpose <chr [1]>
#> 13 movement         read_movement      <chr [2]>
#> 14 octron           read_octron        <chr [1]>
#> 15 sleap            read_sleap         <chr [2]>
#> 16 trackball_bonsai read_trackball     <chr [1]>
#> 17 trackmate        read_trackmate     <chr [1]>
#> 18 trex             read_trex          <chr [2]>
```


:::
:::


You rarely need to call those readers yourself. `read_dataset()` reads any of
these files: it works out which tool wrote it and calls the matching reader.

## Get some data to follow along {#sec-sample}

You don't need your own files. `get_sample_data()` downloads a real export for
any supported source and returns its path:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
path <- get_sample_data("sleap")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr}

```
#> Downloading sleap data...
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
basename(path)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "sleap_single-mouse_EPM.h5"
```


:::
:::


We'll use this recording in all of the guides: ten minutes of a single mouse on
an elevated plus maze, tracked with [SLEAP](https://sleap.ai). To see what else
is available, call `get_sample_data(list_datasets = TRUE)`.

## Read it {#sec-read}


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement <- read_dataset(path)
movement
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # Individuals: individual1
#> # Keypoints:   centre, left_ear, right_ear, snout, tail_base, tail_end
#>    individual  keypoint  time     x     y confidence
#>    <fct>       <fct>    <int> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 individual1 centre       1    NA    NA         NA
#>  2 individual1 centre       2    NA    NA         NA
#>  3 individual1 centre       3    NA    NA         NA
#>  4 individual1 centre       4    NA    NA         NA
#>  5 individual1 centre       5    NA    NA         NA
#>  6 individual1 centre       6    NA    NA         NA
#>  7 individual1 centre       7    NA    NA         NA
#>  8 individual1 centre       8    NA    NA         NA
#>  9 individual1 centre       9    NA    NA         NA
#> 10 individual1 centre      10    NA    NA         NA
#> # i 110,900 more rows
```


:::
:::


## What you got back {#sec-anipoint}

That's an **anipoint**: one row per point (here, each keypoint of each
individual) at each moment. It's one of the *aniframe* classes defined by
[anicore](https://animovement.dev/anicore), which every other package in the
ecosystem reads and returns. Underneath it's a
[tibble](https://tibble.tidyverse.org), so `dplyr` and `ggplot2` work on it as
usual. On top, metadata records what each column is for:

| Question | Role | Read it with | Here |
|----------|------|--------------|------|
| **What** is moving? | identity | `get_variables(movement, "what")` | `individual`, `keypoint` |
| **When**? | index | `get_index(movement)` | `time` |
| **Where**? | position | `get_axes(movement)` | `x`, `y` |


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_variables(movement, "what")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "individual" "keypoint"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
get_index(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "time"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
get_axes(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   x   y 
#> "x" "y"
```


:::
:::


Two consequences worth knowing from the start:

- **Column names are free.** The roles are what matter, so a file whose identity
  column is called `track` works just as well.
- **The frame arrives grouped by identity**, so everything downstream runs
  within each track rather than across them:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
dplyr::n_groups(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] 6
```


:::
:::


Six groups: one mouse × six keypoints. That grouping is why interpolation
never bleeds from the snout into the tail, and why speed is never computed
across the join between two tracks.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Going deeper
This is the short version. anicore's articles cover the data structure in full:
[The aniframe data structure](https://animovement.dev/anicore/articles/aniframe-structure.html)
for the roles and how to set them, and
[Metadata on an aniframe](https://animovement.dev/anicore/articles/aniframe-metadata.html)
for everything below.
:::

## Tell it about your recording {#sec-metadata}

An anipoint keeps context that a bare data frame would lose. The reader fills in
what the file records:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_metadata(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> -- animovement metadata --------------------------------------------------------
#> spec_version: aniframe 3.0.0, anievent 1.0.0
#> 
#> -- recording 
#> source         (character) : "sleap"
#> source_version (character) : <NA>
#> source_format  (character) : "h5"
#> filename       (character) : "sleap_single-mouse_EPM.h5"
#> 
#> -- time 
#> unit_time         (factor)  : "frame"
#>                               [levels: unknown, frame, ns, us, ms, s, m, h]
#> sampling_rate     (numeric) : <NA>
#> sampling_interval (numeric) : 1
#> start_datetime    (POSIXct) : <NA>
#> 
#> -- space 
#> coordinate_system (factor)    : "cartesian_2d"
#>                                 [levels: unknown, cartesian_1d, cartesian_2d, cartesian_3d, polar, cylindrical, spherical]
#> reference_frame   (factor)    : "allocentric"
#>                                 [levels: allocentric, egocentric, none]
#> handedness        (factor)    : "right"
#>                                 [levels: right, left, unknown]
#> axis_directions   (character) : "right, up, back"
#> axis_extents      (numeric)   : 861.2433
#> unit_space        (factor)    : "px"
#>                                 [levels: px, none, nm, um, mm, cm, m, km]
#> unit_angle        (factor)    : "rad"
#>                                 [levels: rad, deg, none]
#> euler_sequence    (character) : <NA>
#> euler_intrinsic   (logical)   : <NA>
#> 
#> -- variables 
#> what   keys: individual, keypoint
#> when   index: time | keys: -
#> where  position: x = x, y = y
#> event  state: - | point: -
#> 
#> -- structure 
#> (empty)
```


:::
:::


Two things are missing that everything downstream depends on: how fast the
camera recorded, and how big a pixel is.

### Time in seconds {#sec-time}

SLEAP's analysis files don't record a frame rate, so `time` counts frames.
Declare the rate, then convert the time column to seconds:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement <- movement |>
  set_metadata(sampling_rate = 30) |>
  convert_unit_time("s")
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## Use your own frame rate
We're assuming 30 fps for this sample. Set whatever your recording actually
was: everything downstream that involves time scales with this number.
:::

### Space in centimetres {#sec-space}

Coordinates are in pixels (`unit_space: px`), which is all a video can tell
you. To get real distances you need something of known size in the picture.
Here we use the mouse itself: an adult mouse measures about 9 cm from its snout
to the base of its tail, and stretched out, this one spans about 140 pixels.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement <- movement |>
  convert_unit_space("cm", calibration_factor = 9 / 140)
```
:::


`convert_unit_space()` rescales every coordinate by that factor and records the
new unit. The header now shows the sampling rate and the duration, and from
here on, distances come out in centimetres and speeds in centimetres per
second:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> # Individuals:   individual1
#> # Keypoints:     centre, left_ear, right_ear, snout, tail_base, tail_end
#> # Sampling rate: 30 Hz
#> # Time:          00:00:00 to 00:10:16
#>    individual  keypoint   time     x     y confidence
#>    <fct>       <fct>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
#>  1 individual1 centre   0.0333    NA    NA         NA
#>  2 individual1 centre   0.0667    NA    NA         NA
#>  3 individual1 centre   0.1       NA    NA         NA
#>  4 individual1 centre   0.133     NA    NA         NA
#>  5 individual1 centre   0.167     NA    NA         NA
#>  6 individual1 centre   0.2       NA    NA         NA
#>  7 individual1 centre   0.233     NA    NA         NA
#>  8 individual1 centre   0.267     NA    NA         NA
#>  9 individual1 centre   0.3       NA    NA         NA
#> 10 individual1 centre   0.333     NA    NA         NA
#> # i 110,900 more rows
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## Calibrate against something in the same plane
For your own recordings, film an object of known size, such as a ruler or the
arena itself, at the height the animal moves at. A rough scale is fine for
following these guides, but measurements are only as good as the calibration
behind them.
:::

## Take a first look {#sec-look}

Calling `plot()` on an anipoint draws the trajectories, with axis labels taken
from the metadata:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Raw SLEAP tracks. The plus maze is clearly visible, and so are a handful of points that landed nowhere near it.](read-data_files/figure-html/first-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


The maze shape comes straight out of the data, with no annotation needed. So do
the long lines reaching off to the left: a few dozen points, out of
110,910, that landed well outside the maze.
They're drawn as long straight lines because the plot joins consecutive
positions. Whether that matters, and what else is hiding in there, is what the
[next guide](check-data.qmd) is for.

## Attach the skeleton {#sec-structure}

Pose-estimation tools also record which keypoints are joined to which: the
skeleton. `read_structure()` reads it from the same file, and `set_structure()`
attaches it to the frame:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
movement <- movement |>
  set_structure(read_structure(path))

get_structure(movement)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> $keypoint
#> <anistructure> 6 points, 7 segments, 0 joints
#> variable: keypoint
#> Points: snout, left_ear, right_ear, centre, tail_base, tail_end
#> Segments: snout-left_ear (snout -> left_ear), snout-right_ear (snout -> right_ear), snout-centre (snout -> centre), left_ear-centre (left_ear -> centre), right_ear-centre (right_ear -> centre), centre-tail_base (centre -> tail_base), tail_base-tail_end (tail_base -> tail_end)
```


:::
:::


With the skeleton attached, functions that work on body segments know what the
segments are. The anicore article on
[structures](https://animovement.dev/anicore/articles/structures.html) covers
them in full.

## Reading your own files {#sec-own}

Point `read_dataset()` at your file. If you're curious what it decides the file
is, `detect_source()` tells you without reading it:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
detect_source(path)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "sleap"
```


:::
:::


When detection can't tell two sources apart, or you want to be explicit, name
the source: `read_dataset(path, source = "sleap")`. Each reader's help page,
such as `?read_sleap`, documents the options specific to that format. Pass them
to `read_dataset()` and it hands them on.

For a format aniread doesn't cover, `read_custom()` maps arbitrary columns onto
the roles above. And once you've read something, `write_aniframe()` saves it to
a Parquet file, metadata and all, which `read_aniframe()` opens again far
faster than re-parsing the original export.

Next: [check what you actually have](check-data.qmd).
